office-logo-concept.body:
## The Design Brief

Create a recognisable arrival point without overpowering the interior. This reception concept pairs a dimensional logo with soft rear illumination, leaving space around the mark so it reads clearly from the entrance.

## Design Decisions

### Light behind the logo

Rear illumination outlines the lettering while keeping the faces visually calm. Wall texture and stand-off distance affect how the halo spreads.

### Finish in conversation with the space

A warm metal appearance works with stone and timber. The final metal, surface treatment and colour reference are selected for your brand.

### Scale around the reception desk

Use the desk width, wall area and entrance sightline to set the overall logo width and position. A wall photograph is more useful than a letter height alone.

## Proposed Configuration

**Application:** Office and reception feature wall

**Letter construction:** Opaque metal face and formed returns; construction to be specified

**Lighting direction:** Rear LED illumination; warm or neutral white to be reviewed

**Finish:** Brushed, painted or plated appearance by approved reference

**Mounting approach:** Stand-off fixing with a planned cable route behind the sign

**Size & scope:** Made to your artwork; dimensions, components and installation scope quoted individually

## Prepare Your Installation

### Check the wall

Send a straight-on photo, available width and height, and wall material. Uneven or reflective finishes can change the halo.

### Plan power and access

Identify the cable exit, driver location and maintenance access with your installer before the wall is closed.

### Review the visual proof

Confirm logo spacing, wall clearance, light colour and the sign position on your wall drawing before production.

## Make It Your Own

Replace the mark and lettering with your own vector artwork. Adjust the overall scale, metal finish and light colour to suit the space.

For multiple reception locations, share a wall photo and dimensions for each site so the same visual direction can be adapted consistently.

hospitality-metal-concept.body:
## The Design Brief

Give a hospitality entrance an understated identity that belongs to the architecture. This concept uses unlit dimensional lettering, with the material finish and surrounding ambient light doing the visual work.

## Design Decisions

### Material takes the lead

A warm brushed-metal appearance creates contrast against the entrance surface. Discuss real finish references rather than relying on a screen colour.

### Depth without integral lighting

Raised lettering casts a changing shadow. Return depth and fixing position need to be balanced with logo size and the viewing angle.

### Room around the identity

The name remains one considered element of the entrance. Align the sign with door, cladding and architectural features.

## Proposed Configuration

**Application:** Hotel, hospitality or commercial entrance

**Letter construction:** Cut or built-up metal, selected to suit the artwork and required depth

**Lighting direction:** Unlit lettering; appearance depends on daylight and site lighting

**Finish:** Brushed, painted or plated surface, subject to finish approval

**Mounting approach:** Stud fixing or a backing arrangement suitable for the substrate

**Size & scope:** Overall width, depth, metal grade and exposed environment to be confirmed

## Prepare Your Installation

### Identify exposure

Tell us whether the location is sheltered, fully outdoors or near the coast. This informs the material and finish review.

### Check the substrate

Provide cladding and wall details so your installer can plan suitable fixings and access.

### Review the light

Include a day and evening site photo. Unlit lettering depends on the lighting already available at the entrance.

## Make It Your Own

Change the font, symbol, metal appearance and dimensional depth. Share a physical or photographed finish reference where colour matching is important.

Coordinate entrance lettering with room, floor or directional signs by including a schedule of the additional items.

## The Design Brief

Bring a brand colour into a bright reception space. The concept uses solid-looking dimensional lettering with a clean outline, relying on colour contrast and depth rather than integral lighting.

## Design Decisions

### Brand colour as the focal point

A saturated colour reads against the pale wall. Confirm the colour reference and whether a painted or material colour is required.

### A simple dimensional silhouette

The artwork should retain clear strokes at the selected size. Review small counters and fine details before agreeing the fabrication approach.

### Daylight and shadow

Unlit lettering uses the room light to reveal depth. The wall and furniture establish the scale of the mark.

## Proposed Configuration

**Application:** Office, studio or reception brand wall

**Letter construction:** Cut or layered acrylic; thickness and assembly to be reviewed

**Lighting direction:** Unlit construction in this concept

**Finish:** Solid colour, surface sheen and edge finish by approved reference

**Mounting approach:** Stud, adhesive or backing option selected for the wall and letter size

**Size & scope:** Artwork, available wall area and letter thickness confirmed before production

## Prepare Your Installation

### Measure the usable wall

Share the wall width and height with any sockets, furniture or features that constrain the layout.

### Discuss fixing limits

Tell us if drilling is restricted. Your installer should confirm the surface and suitable attachment method.

### Approve colour and outline

Send vector artwork and a colour reference. Review cut details and any proposed layering before fabrication.

## Make It Your Own

Adapt the logo, letter colour, thickness and surface sheen. Layer different colours or add a backing panel if required by the design.

If you want illumination, request it explicitly so the material and assembly can be reviewed for that different construction.

marquee-entrance-concept.body:
## The Design Brief

Give a restaurant or entertainment entrance a strong evening identity. This concept combines deep dimensional lettering with visible points of light, using the entrance architecture as a frame.

## Design Decisions

### Light points as part of the identity

The visible lighting rhythm gives the letters their character. Point size, spacing and the artwork need to be designed together.

### Depth and finish add presence

The metal appearance and returns create a substantial silhouette in daylight as well as at night. Confirm the actual material and finish separately.

### Coordinate with the entrance

Review the wall space above the door, adjacent light fittings and the sign viewing angle before setting the final layout.

## Proposed Configuration

**Application:** Restaurant, bar or entertainment entrance

**Letter construction:** Built-up dimensional letters; construction developed around the design

**Lighting direction:** Exposed light points; component type and spacing to be specified

**Finish:** Painted or metal appearance by approved reference

**Mounting approach:** Individual or supported mounting, reviewed against the structure

**Size & scope:** Overall width, return depth, light-point arrangement and access confirmed before quoting

## Prepare Your Installation

### Check fixing and access

Identify the wall construction and how the installer will reach and maintain the sign.

### Review exposure and components

Tell us the destination and whether the sign is exposed to rain. Component selection and required documentation must suit the agreed configuration.

### Confirm the light pattern

Approve a drawing showing letter profiles and light-point positions, together with the finish and cable arrangement.

## Make It Your Own

Change the lettering, finish and light-point arrangement. The design can be adapted for a smaller interior feature or a larger entrance identity.

Include any dimming, replacement-access or event-use requirements at the enquiry stage so they can be reviewed in the quotation.
